messages.subject: understanding profiling Stan
parts:
I've been developing some models which make heavy use of functions to calculate splines and indexes for convenience, and before elaborating things any further, I attached Oprofile to a running model to see if I had some performance-related no-no's.  I did notice that my spline functions show up (part of the Oprofile output below) which suggests I might want to move the weight calculations out when possible (spline weights can be precalculated for this model, as can all the indexes).  It's nice to see that the Oprofile output is so helpful.

add_vv_vari is big---that seems to be from the reverse mode auto-diff for the addition operator and there's not much to do about it for splines or linear models... same goes for divide_vd_vari/sq_vari/exp_vari/etc... except that some of those must be from calculating spline weights (?) Other than the prominence of the spline functions, this seems to square with the general view that most of the time is spent calculating gradients. 

My trying-to-understand-Stan questions: for someone more familiar with profiling Stan---are there any additional lessons here for the model? Are other forms of the Oprofile output more useful for figuring this out?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] understanding profiling Stan
parts:
If addition's taking 15% of your time, you're probably
in very good shape.

> On Jan 18, 2015, at 5:42 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I've been developing some models which make heavy use of functions to calculate splines and indexes for convenience, and before elaborating things any further, I attached Oprofile to a running model to see if I had some performance-related no-no's. I did notice that my spline functions show up (part of the Oprofile output below) which suggests I might want to move the weight calculations out when possible (spline weights can be precalculated for this model, as can all the indexes). It's nice to see that the Oprofile output is so helpful.

Everything that can be calculated in transformed
data should be calculated in transformed data.
Same for generated quantities.
> add_vv_vari is big---that seems to be from the reverse mode auto-diff for the addition operator and there's not much to do about it for splines or linear models...

The biggest thing to do is replace sequences of +=
operations with a vector sum. It's more efficient in
autodiff as it only needs a single virtual function
call and guarantees much more memory locality in the
derivative calcs.

> same goes for divide_vd_vari/sq_vari/exp_vari/etc... except that some of those must be from calculating spline weights (?) Other than the prominence of the spline functions, this seems to square with the general view that most of the time is spent calculating gradients.

Some of these come with transforms. For instance, exp_vari
comes in through the Jacobian for

parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;

which itself needs to be differentiated. Sometimes you can
reparameterize directly with unconstrained variables. We support
that in some cases directly with probability functions like
poisson_log and bernoulli_logit.

If the subtract_vd and divide_vd are coming from probability functions like

y ~ normal(0,1);

then they could probably be sped up if we had a centered_normal
and unit_normal.

> My trying-to-understand-Stan questions: for someone more familiar with profiling Stan---are there any additional lessons here for the model? Are other forms of the Oprofile output more useful for figuring this out?
>

I think that looks pretty good! The time's all being
spent in autodiff derivative propagatins (the chain()
methods), which is what we'd expect.

- Bob

On Sunday, January 18, 2015 at 6:52:55 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
If addition's taking 15% of your time, you're probably
in very good shape.

With your advice below I can see a few places in my code where I can make things go faster.  I suppose the major performance piece not captured by profiling is the number of leapfrog steps required to complete an iteration for this model vs. a simpler one.  The simpler model still does the silly loop over all observations with increment_log_prob, but it runs in minutes rather than hours and profiling doesn't really tell me if that's just due to more parameters or if it's something related to geometry.

Thanks for taking time out of your weekend to answer.... !

Krzysztof

If the subtract_vd and divide_vd are coming from probability functions like

I think that looks pretty good!  The time's all being
spent in autodiff derivative propagatins (the chain()
methods), which is what we'd expect.

- Bob
